Sample Size Planning for Accuracy in Parameter Estimation (AIPE) of the Standardized Mean

Source: R/ss_aipe_sm.R
ss_aipe_sm.Rd

Plans the sample size needed for a sufficiently narrow confidence interval for the population standardized mean, the mean divided by the standard deviation, from the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) perspective.

Usage

ss_aipe_sm(true_sm, width, conf_level = 0.95, assurance = NULL)

Arguments

true_sm

The planning value of the population standardized mean (the population mean divided by the population standard deviation)

width

The desired full width of the obtained confidence interval

conf_level

The desired confidence interval coverage, (i.e., 1 - Type I error rate). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t)

assurance

Optional. The probability that the confidence interval of the planned study is no wider than width: NULL (the default), which plans for the expected width, or a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Any such value may be used. Values such as .80, .90, and .99 are the usual ones, and a value at or below .50 is accepted as well (see Details). Anything else is refused with a condition of class dmar_assurance_invalid. An assurance above .999999998 is refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid: the assurance step finds noncentral t limits with tail areas of (1 - assurance) / 2, which must be at least 1e-9.

Value

A 1-row data.frame with columns term and value:

necessary_N

The necessary total sample size in order to achieve the desired degree of accuracy (i.e., the sufficiently narrow confidence interval)

Details

The plan for the expected width. Without assurance the function finds the smallest sample size at which the noncentral t confidence interval for the standardized mean (ci_sm), computed at true_sm, is no wider than width. The interval of the study itself is computed at the sample standardized mean, which varies from sample to sample, and the interval is wider the larger that value is in magnitude. A plan for the expected width therefore leaves a probability near one half that the interval obtained is wider than width.

The assurance step. With assurance the function follows the one-sample analog of the procedure Kelley and Rausch (2006, Equations 18 to 20 and 25 to 31) give for the standardized mean difference. At the sample size of the plan for the expected width it finds the value that the sample standardized mean exceeds in magnitude with probability 1 - assurance, by a search between the one-sided and the two-sided confidence limits their Equations 25 and 28 name as its bounds, and then plans for the expected width with that value in place of true_sm. That value is defined for every probability strictly between 0 and 1, so every such assurance is accepted. A value above about one half gives a larger sample size than the plan for the expected width, and a value below it gives a smaller one, which is the sample size at which the interval is no wider than width with only that probability: for true_sm = 1, width = 0.5, and 95 percent confidence the function returns 93 without assurance, 93 at .50, 87 at .20, 100 at .80, and 105 at .90. Because the value planned for is found at the first sample size and the returned sample size differs from it, the probability at the returned sample size is near assurance and not exactly it; in that example it is .519, .228, .812, and .925 at the four values of assurance, computed from the noncentral t distribution.

References

Cumming, G., & Finch, S. (2001). A primer on the understanding, use, and calculation of confidence intervals that are based on central and noncentral distributions. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 61(4), 532–574. doi:10.1177/0013164401614002

Hedges, L. V. (1981). Distribution theory for Glass's Estimator of effect size and related estimators. Journal of Educational Statistics, 6(2), 107–128.

Kelley, K. (2005). The effects of nonnormal distributions on confidence intervals around the standardized mean difference: Bootstrap and parametric confidence intervals, Educational and Psychological Measurement, 65, 51–69. doi:10.1177/0013164404264850

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2006). Sample size planning for the standardized mean difference: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Psychological Methods, 11(4), 363–385. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.11.4.363

Steiger, J. H., & Fouladi, R. T. (1997). Noncentrality interval estimation and the evaluation of statistical models. In L. L. Harlow, S. A. Mulaik, & J. H. Steiger (Eds.), What if there were no significance tests? (pp. 221–257). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

See also

ci_nc_t, ci_sm

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Suppose the population mean is believed to be 20, and the population
# standard deviation is believed to be 2; thus the population standardized
# mean is believed to be 10. To determine the necessary sample size for a
# study so that the full width of the 95 percent confidence interval
# obtained in the study will be, with 90% assurance, no wider than 2.5,
# the function should be specified as follows.

ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 10, width = 2.5, conf_level = .95, assurance = .90)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 150  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The plan for the expected width, and the sample size at which the
# interval is no wider than 0.5 with probability .50, for a standardized
# mean of 1.
ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 1, width = 0.5)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 93   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 1, width = 0.5, assurance = .50)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 93   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
